# Discourse Graphs

> Discourse Graphs are an information
> model that represents research as
> questions, claims, and evidence
> connected by typed relations
> (supports, opposes, addresses,
> interpreted-as), rather than as
> documents. The project maintains an
> open interoperability protocol plus
> plugins for Roam Research and
> Obsidian, so researchers can share
> and reuse discourse units across
> tools.

The base schema defines four node
types — Question, Claim, Evidence,
Source — and four relation types —
Supports, Opposes, Addresses,
InterpretedAs. A tool has a discourse
graph, and can interoperate on the
protocol, if it contains data
structures that map to these base
nodes and relations.

Two design commitments constrain
implementations: local label
variations (hypothesis, result,
conclusion) should point to the
nearest base schema node type; and
relations are reified as separate
assertions with their own metadata
rather than attributes of a node.

Maintained by Homeworld Collective.
Licensed Apache 2.0. Supported by
Protocol Labs Research, Chan
Zuckerberg Initiative, Metagov,
Schmidt Futures, and The Navigation
Fund.

## Core concepts

- [What is a discourse graph?](https://discoursegraphs.com/docs/obsidian/fundamentals/what-is-a-discourse-graph):
  Canonical definition of the
  information model, the four node
  types, and three worked examples
  (understanding a problem,
  formulating a contribution,
  constructing a theory).
- [Base grammar](https://discoursegraphs.com/docs/obsidian/fundamentals/base-grammar):
  The fixed relational vocabulary —
  question, claim, evidence, source,
  and the relations between them.
- [Conceptual schema draft](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/schemas/blob/main/conceptual-schema-draft.md):
  Full specification of the base
  schema, guiding principles,
  documented local variations (lab,
  HCI, UX research), and technical
  instantiations.

## Documentation

- [Documentation home](https://discoursegraphs.com/docs):
  Entry point; splits by client.
- [Roam Research plugin docs](https://discoursegraphs.com/docs/roam):
  Installation, graph building,
  querying, advanced workflows.
- [Obsidian plugin docs](https://discoursegraphs.com/docs/obsidian):
  Setup, node and relation authoring,
  sync, workspace configuration.

## Schemas and technical specs

- [Schemas repository](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/schemas):
  All technical instantiations of the
  conceptual schema.
- [OWL ontology (dg_core.ttl)](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/schemas/blob/main/owl/dg_core.ttl):
  Minimal shared set of nodes and
  relations, mapped to SEPIO,
  micropublications, and ScholOnto.
- [ATProto Lexicon](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/schemas/blob/main/atproto-lexicon):
  Prototype `org.discoursegraphs.*`
  lexicon mapping the base schema to
  federated ATProto records, with
  reified relations carrying their own
  authorship and provenance.
- [MyST specification](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/schemas/blob/main/discourse-graphs-myst-spec.md):
  Draft MyST Markdown directives and
  roles embedding discourse graph
  semantics into scientific documents.

## Source code

- [Main monorepo](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph):
  Roam plugin and website.
- [Obsidian plugin](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph-obsidian)

## Background reading

- [Steps Towards an Infrastructure for Scholarly Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.20666v2):
  Preprint on discourse graph plugin
  design and use cases.
- [Knowledge synthesis: conceptual model and practical guide](https://oasislab.pubpub.org/pub/54t0y9mk/release/3)
